title: Djisktra's Algorithm
problemStatement: Single-source shortest paths on a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. Return dist[0…n-1] (∞ / −1 for unreachable).
intuition: Greedily settle the closest unsettled node (BFS with a min-heap instead of FIFO). Needs non-negative weights. Negatives → use Bellman-Ford (a different algorithm, not a “brute” Dijkstra).

approaches.title: Brute: O(n²) Dijkstra (scan for min each time)
approaches.idea: Same greedy: repeatedly pick the unsettled node with smallest dist by scanning an array — no heap. Correct, slow on sparse graphs.
limitations: Not Bellman-Ford — that is for negatives / cycle detect

approaches.title: Better: Dijkstra with min-heap (priority queue)
approaches.idea: dist[], heap of (d,u); skip stale entries (d != dist[u]). Default interview solution in Python/Java/C++.
approaches.time: O((n + m) log n) with binary heap
approaches.dryRun: Settle nodes in increasing distance order; once popped with dist[u], it is final (non-negative weights).
approaches.whyWorks: Non-negative weights ⇒ no future path can improve a settled node.
limitations: Negative edge → WRONG — use Bellman-Ford instead
May keep stale (d,u) pairs in the heap

approaches.title: Optimal: ordered set (C++ set / Java TreeSet)
approaches.idea: std::set and TreeSet keep {dist, node} in ascending order, so begin()/first() is always the closest unsettled label — same role as a min-heap. On improve you erase the old {dist[v], v} then insert the new pair (fewer stale keys than PQ). Python’s built-in set is unordered — stay on the Better (heapq) version.
approaches.whyWorks: Ordered set’s smallest element = closest-first, same greedy as the PQ version, with explicit erase of outdated keys.
limitations: Python: no std::set equivalent in the stdlib for this — use heapq (Better)

python.notes: Use heapq only. Python’s set is unordered — you cannot mirror C++ set / Java TreeSet Dijkstra with the built-in set. (SortedList is 3rd-party.)

java.notes: TreeSet keeps {dist,node} ascending — same idea as C++ set. Prefer PriorityQueue in most Java interviews; TreeSet erase/insert avoids stale keys.

cpp.notes: set keeps pairs sorted ascending — begin() is closest. Erase old {dist[v],v} before insert to avoid duplicates. PQ also works (stale skips).

specialTechnique.title: PQ vs ordered set vs Python
specialTechnique.body:
Closest-first structure options:
• C++ priority_queue / Java PriorityQueue — allow duplicate keys; skip if d != dist[u]
• C++ set / Java TreeSet — ordered ascending; erase+insert on improve (fewer stale entries)
• Python — use heapq only. Built-in set is unordered, so the set-based Dijkstra pattern does not apply.

Algorithm choice:
Unweighted → BFS
Non-negative weights → Dijkstra
Negative edges / neg-cycle → Bellman-Ford
0/1 weights → 0-1 BFS
DAG → topo + relax

commonMistakes: Labeling Bellman-Ford as brute force for this problem
followUps: K shortest paths / constraints on stops?
interviewInsight: State the weight assumption before coding. If negatives appear, switch algorithms — don’t call Bellman-Ford a brute.
